question.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Curve
question.problem: Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve $r(t)={t}^{3}\,i+3t\,j+{t}^{4}\,k$ from  $t=2$ to $t=5?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4})\,k \\  & =3{t}^{2}\,i+3\,j+4{t}^{3}\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(3{t}^{2})^{2}+(3)^{2}+(4{t}^{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+9+16{t}^{6}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{2}^{5}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t={\int }_{2}^{5}\sqrt{16{t}^{6}+9{t}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For q-127602, the speed is t^2+1, whose integral from -1 to 2 is 6. For q-77220, differentiation gives (4t cos(2t),4t sin(2t)), so the speed is 4t on [1,2] and the length is 6. Its source contains an intermediate typographical error that drops the doubled trigonometric arguments and leaves sine without an argument; the corrected calculation still confirms its final answer. For q-76906 and q-33779, integrating the speeds 2sqrt(2)t and 2t gives 4sqrt(2) and 8. The inverse-trigonometric integrals follow by substituting x/3, sqrt(3)x, x/3, 3x, sqrt(3)x, 4x, and 2x respectively; the arcsec derivatives include the required absolute value. For q-15405, y'=4sin(2x), giving the displayed arc-length integrand. For q-6001, y'=ln(x)+1, and expanding 1+(ln(x)+1)^2 gives the selected expression. For q-85665, the speed is (e^x+e^(-x))/2, whose integral over [0,ln(2)] is 3/4.
